title: The watchman (Ezekiel 33:1–9)
hookLine: a watchman must warn, whether or not anyone listens

lines: WHO IS SUPPOSED TO SAY SOMETHING?
A MAN ON THE CITY WALL.
cards: Who is supposed to say something? A smoke alarm chirping in the apartment next door. A friend about to drive home after too many drinks.
A coworker about to send an email to the wrong list. Each is the same moment: knowing something the other person doesn't, and wondering whose place it is to speak.
Ezekiel 33 opens with exactly that question, set on a city wall. A city chooses one of its people and sets him up high to watch the road. When he sees danger coming, he blows the trumpet.

teach.b: The chapter lays it out like a case of law, two ways.

teach.h: NO TRUMPET, AND THE WATCHMAN ANSWERS.
teach.b: First case: the watchman sees the sword coming and blows the trumpet. Someone hears it and ignores it, and the sword takes him; his blood is on his own head. The watchman did his part.
Second case: the watchman sees the sword coming and stays quiet. Then the responsibility falls on the watchman.

Then God turns the picture toward Ezekiel himself, in the King James words: "So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me."
And if you warn, and the person does not turn, "thou hast delivered thy soul." The watchman is responsible for seeing and for speaking, not for what people do with the warning. That can be a relief.
It also takes away every excuse for silence. And the warning isn't meant as a threat.
A few verses later comes the reason for all of it: "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live." The point of the trumpet is not to be right.

teach.h: THE POINT IS THAT PEOPLE LIVE.
teach.b: The point is that people live. Jewish ethics has its own form of this. The Torah says, do not stand idly by the blood of your neighbor, and the rabbis read it as a duty to act when someone is in danger.
A watchman isn't a scold. He's someone who cares enough to make a sound.

how: Jews read Ezekiel 33 among the Latter Prophets; the duty to warn and to act when someone is in danger is also taught from the Torah's command not to stand idly by a neighbor's blood.

a guard who arrests anyone breaking the law
one set on the wall to warn of danger

his blood is on his own head

s: the watchman is blamed if people ignore his warning
if he warns and they don't turn, the text says he has delivered his soul.

the watchman's job includes making people listen
his job is to see and to sound the trumpet; what they do is theirs.

games.q: you're the watchman. you see the sword coming, and you know half the city won't listen. what do you do?
o: stay quiet: they won't listen anyway.
warn only the people you like.
games.why: the text is clear: blow the trumpet. if they ignore it, their blood is on their own head; if you stay silent, the responsibility is yours.

practice: Ask yourself whether there's a warning you've been sitting on: someone running too hard, a risk a friend can't see, a tire that looks low.

Find the one sentence and, in your mind, say it kindly, without blame, the way you'd want to hear it. Notice that after you say it, the choice is theirs; if you pray, you can bring that person before God.

wordCard.voice: The watchman. Set on the wall to see danger and blow the trumpet; Ezekiel is told he is the watchman for his people. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: watchman, one who looks out from a high place.

carryVoice: Your line: the watchman warns. What they do with the warning is up to them. Until tomorrow.
